seoTitle: ATLAW Case Results: Michigan Personal Injury Settlements and Verdicts
seoDescription: Settlements and verdicts recovered by ATLAW for injured people across Michigan: no-fault benefits, catastrophic injury, and product injury cases, with the case type, county, and year for each, and a plain explanation of what drives case value in Michigan.
tagline: More than $100 million recovered across more than 10,000 cases in 13 years. Here is what some of those cases looked like.
primaryKeyword: atlaw case results (branded; no measurable volume)

c.v: In 13 years, ATLAW has handled more than 10,000 cases for injured people in Michigan and recovered more than $100 million for them. The results below are a selection from those cases, and more will be added. Each lists the type of case, the county where it arose, the year it resolved, how it ended, and a short description of what happened, so you can find the cases that resemble yours.

Two things to read before the numbers. First, every amount shown is the gross recovery, before attorney fees, case costs, and the repayment of medical liens; what a client takes home is less, and the section on fees and liens below explains how much less and why. Second, no past result predicts a future one. Michigan law caps some damages and not others, limits recovery to the at-fault driver’s insurance in most crash cases, and reduces or bars recovery when the injured person shares fault. The same injury can resolve for very different amounts depending on facts that have nothing to do with how badly someone was hurt. The section on what drives case value explains those facts.

c.v: $833,101 for a vehicle component explosion that destroyed an eye.

Our client was driving home from work when he heard a strange noise from under the hood. He pulled over and opened the hood to find the source, and a component exploded into his face. The impact detached the retina, tore the iris, and destroyed the lens of his left eye, fractured bone, and cracked his teeth. The injury happened in November 2019, and the claim was resolved in Wayne County.

Our client was three years old, riding in the back seat, when a 1988 crash left him with a traumatic brain injury and quadriplegia. For years his no-fault insurer paid for round-the-clock attendant care, but after Michigan’s 2019 no-fault reform it cut his paid care to eight hours a day. We filed suit in Wayne County in 2024 to recover the benefits, and the case settled. One further payment is expected.

sections.heading: What these results mean, and what they do not

c.v: A settlement is an agreement; a verdict is a decision. Most Michigan injury cases settle, often after suit is filed and the insurer has seen the medical records and depositions, sometimes at a court-ordered case evaluation or facilitation. A jury verdict is the amount a jury awarded after trial; the judgment entered on it may be higher, with interest and costs, or lower after reductions for the plaintiff’s share of fault or statutory caps, and it may be appealed. An arbitration award is a decision by a private arbitrator, common in uninsured and underinsured motorist claims where the policy requires it. Where a result says “policy limits,” the insurer paid the full amount of coverage available, which is the most it can be made to pay regardless of what the injury was worth.
Gross is not net. Michigan court rules cap the contingency fee in personal injury cases at one-third of the recovery (MCR 8.121).

Case costs, such as filing fees, record charges, deposition transcripts, and expert witnesses, are repaid from the recovery, and in a litigated case with experts they can be substantial. Medical providers, health insurers, Medicare, and Medicaid that paid for crash-related treatment usually have a right to be repaid from a third-party recovery, under federal law for Medicare (42 USC 1395y(b)(2)) and Michigan law for Medicaid (MCL 400.106), and ERISA health plans assert reimbursement under their plan terms. Part of a lawyer’s work on any case is reducing those liens before distribution. Ask any firm you consult to show you, in writing, how the fee, costs, and liens would come out of a hypothetical recovery.
The amount reflects the coverage as much as the injury. See below.

sections.heading: What drives case value in Michigan

c.v: Michigan is a no-fault state with its own rules, and several of them explain why two people with the same injury can recover very different amounts.
No-fault benefits come first, from your own insurer, regardless of fault.

Under MCL 500.3107, your own policy pays medical expenses up to the PIP level you selected ($50,000 for Medicaid enrollees, $250,000, $500,000, or unlimited since the 2019 reform), 85 percent of lost wages for up to three years (capped at $7,201 a month for the year beginning October 2025), replacement services at $20 a day, and attendant care. These are paid as bills come due, not as a lump sum, so they rarely appear as a “settlement” unless the insurer denied them and the firm sued. A no-fault case result is usually the recovery of denied or cut-off benefits plus 12 percent penalty interest under MCL 500.3142 and attorney fees under MCL 500.3148.
The claim against the at-fault driver requires a threshold injury.

Under MCL 500.3135, you can sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering only if you suffered death, a serious impairment of body function, or permanent serious disfigurement. Economic losses beyond what no-fault pays (wages above the monthly cap or beyond three years, for example) can also be claimed. If the injury does not meet the threshold, there is no pain-and-suffering claim, however real the pain.
The at-fault driver’s policy limits are usually the ceiling.

Michigan’s minimum liability coverage is $50,000 per person and $100,000 per crash under MCL 500.3009(1), and many drivers carry the minimum; a severe injury caused by a minimally insured driver recovers $50,000 from that driver’s insurer unless the driver has personal assets, which is rare. Underinsured motorist coverage on your own policy pays the difference up to your UIM limit; uninsured motorist coverage stands in for a driver with no insurance or a hit-and-run. Whether a client bought UM/UIM coverage, and how much, is often the single largest factor in the size of a crash recovery. Commercial trucks carry federal minimums of $750,000 and often far more (49 CFR 387.9), which is why truck-crash results tend to be larger than car-crash results for similar injuries.
Fault is shared, and it reduces the recovery.

Under MCL 600.2959 and 500.3135(2)(b), a plaintiff’s damages are reduced by the plaintiff’s percentage of fault, and a plaintiff more than 50 percent at fault recovers no pain-and-suffering damages at all. A disputed left turn or a pedestrian outside a crosswalk changes the number.
Some damages are capped; most are not.

Michigan has no cap on pain-and-suffering damages in car, truck, premises, or dog-bite cases. Medical malpractice noneconomic damages are capped under MCL 600.1483 at $596,400 for 2026, or $1,065,000 for the most severe categories of injury, adjusted each year. Claims against government entities (a city bus, a county road) are limited by the Governmental Tort Liability Act, with its own notice requirements and short deadlines (MCL 691.1401 et seq.).
The injury type and the medical record.

Documented objective injury, consistent treatment, and a clear causal link to the crash in the records drive value; gaps in treatment, prior similar complaints, and symptoms with no imaging to support them reduce it. This is why we tell every client to
see a doctor the day of the crash and keep every appointment
Who the defendant is.

A premises case against a national retailer with a $5 million policy and a premises case against a homeowner with a $100,000 policy are valued differently. A dog bite in Michigan is strict liability under MCL 287.351, but the recovery is almost always the homeowner’s or renter’s policy limit.
Time.

Cases that settle before suit resolve faster for less; cases tried to verdict take two to three years and carry the risk of a defense verdict. The right choice depends on the facts, the coverage, and what the client needs.

People search for the average car accident settlement in Michigan, and websites supply numbers, usually $15,000 to $30,000 for a “minor” injury and six figures for a “serious” one, with no source. There is no public database of Michigan settlements; nearly all are confidential. The published figures are either a firm’s own selected results or an estimate. The honest answer is that a Michigan crash claim is worth the lesser of what the injury would be valued at by a jury in that county and the insurance available to pay it, reduced by any share of fault, and that the only way to know is to have a lawyer review the police report, the medical records, and every policy that might apply. That review is free.

faqs.question: Are these all of ATLAW’s results?

answer.v: No. They are a selection from more than 10,000 cases. Most settlements are confidential, and many clients prefer that their cases not be described publicly even without names. The firm’s total recovery, more than $100 million, includes every matter.

faqs.question: Are the amounts before or after fees?

answer.v: Before. Every figure is the gross recovery. Fees (capped at one-third in Michigan personal injury cases), case costs, and medical liens come out of the gross. Ask us to show you how that works for your case before you sign anything.

faqs.question: Is there an average settlement for a car accident in Michigan?

answer.v: Not a reliable one. Settlements are confidential and depend on the injury, the threshold, the available insurance, and fault. Any website quoting an average is estimating or describing its own cases.

faqs.question: Why do truck cases recover more than car cases?

answer.v: Mostly coverage: federal law requires interstate carriers to carry at least $750,000 in liability coverage, and many carry $1 million or more, while Michigan’s minimum for a car is $50,000 per person.

faqs.question: How long did these cases take?

answer.v: From a few months for a policy-limits settlement to three years or more for a case tried to verdict.
